meta.title: Tokenization and Context Windows
meta.thesis: A language model never sees your words — it sees tokens, and it can only hold a fixed number of them at once (the context window). Understanding both explains model cost, why long inputs get truncated, and how to budget what you send.

mentalMap.oneLineThesis: Text becomes tokens, tokens fill a fixed context window, and that window's size drives cost, truncation, and what you can send.

nodes.orient: Why models split text into tokens instead of words or letters.
nodes.sub: The unit a model actually reads — not words, not characters.
nodes.what: A token is the chunk of text a model encodes; usually a word-piece, not a whole word.
nodes.relevance: Everything else (cost, limits, truncation) is measured in tokens, so this is the base unit.

nodes.sub: How many tokens the model can attend to at once.
nodes.what: The context window is the maximum number of tokens (prompt plus reply) a model processes per call.
nodes.relevance: It sets a hard ceiling on how much you can send and how long a reply can be.

nodes.relevance: Tokens cost money and the window is finite, so every prompt is a budgeting decision.

nodes.relevance: Knowing how the window fails is what turns the concept into a reliable habit.

modules.title: What a token is
modules.sub: Starts the spine: the unit a model actually reads.
modules.summary: A model never sees your characters or words directly — it sees tokens, small word-pieces produced by a tokenizer. This module explains what a token is and why models work this way before we count them.
objectives: Explain what a token is and how it differs from a word or a character.
Describe why models use sub-word tokens instead of whole words.
Estimate roughly how many tokens a short English passage uses.

spans.text: Why this exists:

a model can only do math on numbers, not letters. Tokenization is the step that turns your text into a sequence of numbered pieces the model can process. Almost every practical limit you hit — cost, length caps, truncation — is counted in those pieces, so it pays to know what they are.
Before reading on, predict:
if you typed the word "unbelievable", do you think the model reads it as one piece, or several? Hold your guess.

blocks.title: A token is a piece of text, not a word
blocks.analogy: Think of tokens like LEGO bricks for language: common words are one brick, but a rarer word like "unbelievable" gets built from a few bricks ("un", "bel", "iev", "able").

spans.text: When you send text to an
LLM
, it is first split by a
tokenizer
into a list of
tokens
. A token is usually a common word or a word-piece — not always a whole word, and not a single letter.

items.text: Common words are usually one token:
"the", "cat", and "run" are each a single token.
Rare or long words split into several:
"unbelievable" may become "un" + "believ" + "able".
Spaces and punctuation count too:
a leading space is often part of the token, and "." or "," can be their own token.

spans.text: A useful rule of thumb for English: about
1 token ≈ 4 characters ≈ ¾ of a word
. So 100 words is roughly 130 tokens. (The answer to the prediction above: "unbelievable" is usually several tokens, not one.)

blocks.title: Granularity: characters → tokens → words
blocks.caption: Slide to see the unit a model could split text on, and why sub-word tokens are the practical middle ground.

stops.label: Characters
stops.note: Every letter is a unit. The vocabulary is tiny, but sequences get extremely long and the model loses word-level meaning.

stops.label: Sub-word tokens (what models use)
stops.note: Common words stay whole; rare words split into reusable pieces. Balances a manageable vocabulary with short sequences. This is the real choice.

stops.label: Whole words
stops.note: Short sequences, but the vocabulary explodes and any unseen word (a typo, a name) has no token at all.

spans.text: Take the sentence:
"Tokenizers split unbelievable words."
A typical tokenizer might break it into these eight tokens (a leading space is shown as ·):

items.text: "Token"
"izers"
— even a common-looking word can split into a stem plus an ending.
" split"
— one token, with its leading space attached.
" un"
"believ"
"able"
— the rare word "unbelievable" becomes three pieces.
" words"
— the period is its own token.

spans.text: Five English words became eight tokens. That gap is exactly why you should count tokens rather than words when a limit matters.

blocks.title: How the tokenizer learns its pieces

spans.text: Modern tokenizers use an algorithm such as Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE). It starts from individual bytes and repeatedly merges the most frequently adjacent pair into a new token, building a fixed vocabulary (often 50,000–100,000 tokens).
Practical consequence: the same tokenizer is used to encode AND decode, so the model and your token-counting tool must use the model's own tokenizer. Counting with the wrong one gives wrong numbers.

blocks.prompt: Which statement best describes what a token is?

options.text: A piece of text — often a word or a word-fragment — that the model encodes as a number.

blocks.explanation: Tokens are sub-word pieces. Common words are usually one token; rare or long words split into several. They are not characters and not always whole words.

modules.title: The context window
modules.sub: Follows tokens: how many of them the model can hold at once.
modules.summary: Now that text is tokens, the next question is how many the model can process in a single call. That ceiling is the context window — and it counts both your prompt and the model's reply.
objectives: Define the context window as a fixed token budget per request.
Explain that the window holds the prompt AND the generated reply together.
Recognize what happens when input exceeds the window.

spans.text: Quick recall from module 1:
before reading on, what is the rough rule of thumb for English — about how many tokens is one word?
Answer: roughly
1 word ≈ 1.3 tokens
(or 1 token ≈ ¾ of a word). Hold that number — you will use it in a moment to check whether text fits the window.

blocks.title: The window is a fixed token budget
blocks.analogy: The context window is like a whiteboard of a fixed size: you can write a lot, but once it's full, nothing more fits — and whatever the model writes back has to share the same board.

spans.text: A
context window
is the maximum number of
tokens
a model can take in for a single request. It is a hard limit set by the model, commonly 8K, 128K, or up to ~1M tokens depending on the model.
The crucial part beginners miss:
the window holds the
prompt
AND the reply together. If the window is 8,000 tokens and your prompt is 7,500, the model has at most 500 tokens left to answer in.

items.text: Input tokens:
your instructions, the conversation history, any documents you paste in.
Output tokens:
everything the model generates back.
Both share one budget:
input + output must fit inside the window.

blocks.title: Filling the window
blocks.caption: Slide to see how much of an 8K-token window the prompt uses — and how little room is left for the reply.

stops.label: Plenty of room
stops.note: Prompt uses 1,000 tokens; about 7,000 remain for the reply. Comfortable for long answers.

stops.label: Getting tight
stops.note: Prompt uses 6,000 tokens; ~2,000 left. A long reply may get cut off mid-sentence.

stops.label: Almost no output room
stops.note: Prompt uses 7,900 tokens; only ~100 left for the reply. The model can barely answer.

blocks.title: Worked example: does this document fit?

spans.text: You want to summarize a 10,000-word report using a model with an 8,000-token window.

items.text: Estimate the input:
Compare to the window:
13,000 > 8,000 — it does not fit, even before leaving room for the summary.
The fix:
split the report into chunks that each fit, summarize each, then summarize the summaries (a "map-reduce" approach).

spans.text: The window is why "just paste the whole thing in" stops working past a certain size — and why chunking exists.

Bigger windows are not free. The transformer's attention compares tokens against each other, so cost grows steeply as the window grows. A larger window also means more input tokens to pay for and slower responses.
So "use the biggest window" is rarely the right default — match the window to the job, and keep the prompt lean.

blocks.prompt: A model has an 8,000-token context window. Your prompt is 7,800 tokens. What is the main problem?

options.text: The prompt is rejected because prompts can use at most half the window.
Only about 200 tokens are left for the reply, so the answer will be very short or cut off.
Nothing — the reply gets its own separate window.

blocks.explanation: The window is shared by input and output. A 7,800-token prompt leaves only ~200 tokens for the reply, so the model cannot produce a full answer.

modules.title: Counting and budgeting tokens
modules.sub: Follows the window: choose what to send so it fits and stays cheap.
modules.summary: The window is finite and tokens cost money, so every request is a budgeting decision. This module is about estimating token counts and choosing how to split the window between input and output.
objectives: Estimate token counts for a prompt before sending it.
Reserve output room so the reply isn't truncated.
Choose a strategy when content is too big for the window.

blocks.title: Every prompt is a budget
blocks.analogy: Budgeting tokens is like packing a fixed-size suitcase: you can't bring everything, so you decide what's essential, what to compress, and how much space to leave for what you'll buy on the trip (the reply).

spans.text: Because the
context window
is fixed and you usually pay per
token
, building a
prompt
means answering three questions:

items.text: How many tokens does my input use?
Estimate (words × 1.3) or count exactly with the model's tokenizer.
How many tokens does the reply need?
Reserve that room up front — set a max-output limit.
What do I cut if it doesn't fit?
Trim history, summarize, or retrieve only the relevant passages instead of pasting everything.

blocks.title: How to budget a request, step by step

spans.text: Count the tokens in your system instructions and any required context. These are non-negotiable and come out of the budget first.
Decide the longest reply you need (e.g. 800 tokens) and subtract it from the window. The rest is what's left for variable input.
Fill the remaining budget with the highest-value content. If it overflows, summarize or retrieve only the relevant pieces rather than truncating blindly.

blocks.title: What to do when content is too big for the window

options.name: Truncate (cut the overflow)

cells.text: Always fits — you just drop tokens past the limit.
High — you may cut the most important part without noticing.

options.whenToUse: Only for clearly-trailing, low-value text (e.g. boilerplate footers).

options.name: Summarize then send

cells.text: Fits, since the summary is far smaller.
Extra model calls to produce summaries.
Medium — detail is compressed but the gist survives.

options.whenToUse: When you need the overall meaning of a large document, not exact wording.

options.name: Retrieve only relevant chunks

cells.text: Fits — you send only the passages that match the question.
Needs a search/retrieval step over chunks.
Low for the question at hand, if retrieval is good.

options.whenToUse: When the answer lives in a small part of a large corpus (the typical RAG case).

blocks.howToRead: Pick the smallest-effort option whose information-loss risk you can accept for THIS task. Default to retrieval when exact details matter.

blocks.prompt: You need exact figures from one section of a 200-page manual. Which budgeting strategy fits best?

options.text: Truncate the manual to the first 8K tokens.
Retrieve only the relevant section and send that.
Summarize the whole manual into a paragraph.

blocks.explanation: When you need exact details from a small part of a large source, retrieval keeps the relevant text intact while fitting the window. Truncation risks cutting the section; summarizing loses the exact figures.

modules.decisionItForces: When content exceeds the window, choose how to fit it: truncate, summarize, or retrieve only the relevant chunks.

modules.title: Counting tokens in code
modules.sub: Follows budgeting: turn the estimate into a real, checkable number.
modules.summary: Eyeballing token counts is unreliable. This module shows a tiny, runnable sketch that counts tokens with the model's own tokenizer before you send a request, and how to sanity-check AI-generated counting code.
objectives: Read a minimal token-counting snippet and explain each line.
Predict the token count of a short string before running it.
Verify AI-generated counting code uses the correct tokenizer.

spans.text: The (words × 1.3) rule is fine for a quick gut-check, but it's wrong for code, non-English text, and unusual formatting. To know for sure, run the text through the model's
tokenizer
and read the real
token
count.
Before reading the code, predict:
how many tokens do you think the string "Hello, world!" is — 1, 3, or 4?

blocks.title: Minimal token counter
blocks.code:
import tiktoken

# Load the tokenizer that matches your model.
enc = tiktoken.encoding_for_model("gpt-4o")

text = "Hello, world!"
tokens = enc.encode(text)        # text -> list of token ids
print(len(tokens))               # how many tokens this text uses

# Fits a budget?
MAX_INPUT = 7000
assert len(tokens) <= MAX_INPUT, "Prompt too long for the window!"

spans.text: This loads the model's own tokenizer, encodes the text into token ids, and reports the count. The
assert
line is the cheap guardrail: it fails loudly before you spend a request on an over-limit prompt.

predictThenReveal.prompt: How many tokens is "Hello, world!" — and which characters become their own tokens?
predictThenReveal.answer: Four tokens: "Hello", ",", " world", "!". The comma and exclamation mark are separate tokens, and " world" carries its leading space.

syntax.explains: Picks the exact tokenizer that model uses — the count is only correct if this matches.
Turns the string into the list of integer token ids the model would see.
The token count — what you compare against the window and what you're billed on.
A guardrail that stops the request early if the prompt won't fit.

spans.text: Verify AI-generated counting code before you trust its numbers.
When an assistant writes token-counting code for you, check these four things:

items.text: Right tokenizer?
It must match your actual model. Counting GPT text with a Llama tokenizer gives wrong numbers.
Counts input AND output?
A budget check that ignores the reply will still overflow the window.
Handles the leading space / special tokens?
Chat models add hidden formatting tokens per message; a raw string count undercounts.
Fails loudly, not silently?
There should be an assert or check, not a comment that says "should be fine".

blocks.prompt: An assistant gives you token-counting code that uses a different model's tokenizer than the one you'll call. What's the risk?

options.text: None — all tokenizers produce the same counts.
The counts can be off, so a prompt you think fits may actually exceed the window.
The code will refuse to run.

blocks.explanation: Different models tokenize differently, so the same text yields different token counts. Using the wrong tokenizer gives a misleading number and you can still overflow the real window.

modules.title: When it breaks, and a check
modules.sub: Closes the spine: the failure modes, then active recall.
modules.summary: Knowing the happy path isn't enough. This module covers the classic ways tokenization and context windows bite in practice — silent truncation, the lost middle, and runaway cost — then a short self-check to lock it in.
objectives: Name the three most common context-window failure modes.
Explain why long inputs can be ignored even when they technically fit.
Recall the token rule of thumb and the shared-budget idea from earlier modules.

spans.text: Before reading on, predict from memory:
in module 2 we said the context window holds two things that share one budget. What are they?
Answer: the
prompt
(input) and the reply (output) share the same window. Keep that in mind — the first failure mode below is exactly what happens when you forget it.

blocks.title: How tokens and windows break in practice

spans.text: These three failures cause most real-world surprises with
context windows
1. Silent truncation (the output gets cut)
The prompt is so large that almost no room is left for the reply. The model stops mid-sentence and the answer looks complete but isn't. Fix: reserve output tokens up front.
2. Lost in the middle (it fits but gets ignored)

Even when a long input fits, models attend most strongly to the beginning and end. Information buried in the middle of a very long prompt is often effectively ignored — so "it fit" does not mean "it was used". Fix: put the most important text near the start or end, and don't over-stuff the window.
3. Runaway cost (token sprawl)
In a chat loop, the whole history is re-sent every turn, so
token
usage — and cost — grows with each message. A long conversation quietly becomes expensive. Fix: trim or summarize old turns instead of carrying everything.
Diagnostic signal:
if a model ignores an instruction you definitely included, suspect either truncation (it was cut) or lost-in-the-middle (it was buried), not that the model "can't follow directions".

blocks.useWhen: A conversation or input is growing long and you must decide what to keep in the window each turn.
blocks.avoidWhen: The whole input is small and comfortably under the window — trimming then just adds complexity for no benefit.
blocks.ruleOfThumb: Keep the system instructions and the most recent, most relevant turns; summarize or drop the rest. Always leave headroom for the reply.

blocks.prompt: You pasted a long instruction into the middle of a very large prompt that fit the window, but the model ignored it. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The instruction was truncated because the prompt didn't fit.
"Lost in the middle" — the model attends most to the start and end, so buried text gets ignored.
The model can't follow instructions at all.

blocks.explanation: If the prompt fit but a middle instruction was ignored, the cause is usually lost-in-the-middle. Move critical instructions toward the start or end, and avoid over-stuffing the window.

modules.decisionItForces: As a conversation grows, decide what to keep in the window each turn: full history, trimmed history, or a running summary.

llm.label: LLM
llm.laymanDefinition: A model trained to predict and generate sequences of tokens, used for text tasks.
llm.technicalNote: In this lesson, the LLM is the consumer of tokens: it reads a token sequence (the context) and generates more tokens.

token.label: Token
token.laymanDefinition: A small piece of text — usually a word or word-fragment — that a model encodes as a number.
token.technicalNote: Tokens are integer ids drawn from a fixed vocabulary; English averages about 1 token per ¾ word.

tokenization.label: Tokenization
tokenization.laymanDefinition: The step that splits text into tokens before a model can process it.
tokenization.technicalNote: Commonly done with sub-word algorithms like Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE) that merge frequent character pairs into a fixed vocabulary.

context_window.label: Context window
context_window.laymanDefinition: The maximum number of tokens a model can take in for a single request, shared by the prompt and the reply.
context_window.technicalNote: A hard per-call limit (e.g. 8K–1M tokens); attention cost grows with the number of tokens in the window.

prompt.label: Prompt
prompt.laymanDefinition: The input text you send to a model — instructions, history, and any pasted content.
prompt.technicalNote: Prompt tokens are the input half of the context window; their count is subtracted from the budget before the reply is generated.

schema.label: Schema
schema.laymanDefinition: A written description of the exact shape data must have.
schema.technicalNote: In this lesson, a budget check is a tiny schema-like constraint: token count must stay under the window limit.

tool_call.label: Tool call
tool_call.laymanDefinition: A structured request from a model to run an external function.
tool_call.technicalNote: Not central to this lesson; included because tool definitions and their results also consume context-window tokens.

questions.q: Your content is larger than the model's context window. What do you do?
questions.why: Truncating blindly can silently drop the most important part of the input.
questions.rot: Prefer retrieval when exact details matter; summarize when only the gist matters.

spans.text: Reconstruct the chain from memory before reading on:

text becomes ____, those fill a fixed ____ shared by prompt and reply, so every request is a ____ decision, which you verify by ____ the tokens, while watching for truncation, lost-in-the-middle, and runaway cost.
The fill-ins: tokens → context window → budgeting → counting. If you can rebuild that sentence, you have the lesson.

When content was too big, did you choose truncate / summarize / retrieve deliberately?

capstone.prompt: Solo build: write a short script that takes a long document and a target model, estimates its token count with the model's tokenizer, reports whether it fits the window with room for a 1,000-token reply, and — if not — picks one strategy (truncate, summarize, or retrieve) and explains why.
